rules.title: Tries to override the AI's instructions
rules.explain: Text that tells the AI to ignore its earlier instructions is the classic prompt-injection pattern. A legitimate add-on has no reason to do this.
rules.fix: Do not install this. If you wrote it, remove the sentence.

rules.title: Tells the AI to hide things from you
rules.explain: Instructions to keep the user in the dark are a strong sign that the add-on wants the AI to do something you would not approve.
rules.fix: Treat as malicious unless you can see a clear, harmless reason.

rules.title: Fake priority or system tags
rules.explain: Tags like <IMPORTANT> or <SYSTEM> inside a tool description are a known trick to make injected text look authoritative to the AI.
rules.fix: Read the text inside the tag. If it gives the AI orders unrelated to the tool's job, do not install.

rules.title: Asks the AI to act silently or without consent
rules.explain: Actions taken silently or without your consent remove you from the loop - exactly what an attacker wants.
rules.fix: Require confirmation for any action this add-on takes.

rules.title: Tries to change the AI's identity or safety mode
rules.explain: Jailbreak-style text tries to switch off the AI's safeguards.
rules.fix: Do not install.

rules.title: Gives orders about other tools (tool shadowing)
rules.explain: A tool that tells the AI how to use *other* tools can hijack them - for example silently changing who an email is sent to.
rules.fix: A tool's description should only describe itself. Review carefully.

rules.title: Claims to be an official instruction
rules.explain: Fake authority is used to pressure the AI (or you) into trusting injected instructions.
rules.fix: Real platform instructions never arrive inside a third-party add-on.

rules.title: Sends data to a known data-collection service
rules.explain: These services are commonly used to receive stolen data. Legitimate add-ons rarely send your data to them.
rules.fix: Find out exactly what is sent there. If it is your data, do not install.

rules.title: Instructs sending your data somewhere
rules.explain: Natural-language instructions to move your files, keys or messages to an outside address are how agent data theft usually works.
rules.fix: Check the destination. Never let an add-on send private data to an address you don't control.

rules.title: Uploads data with curl/wget
rules.explain: Command-line uploads can quietly push local data to a server.
rules.fix: Check what file or data is being uploaded and where to.

rules.title: Encodes data before sending it
rules.explain: Encoding data right before a network call is a common way to hide what is being sent.
rules.fix: Review the code path; there should be a clear, harmless reason.

rules.title: Accesses passwords, keys or private files
rules.explain: These locations hold SSH keys, cloud credentials, passwords, browser logins or crypto wallets. An add-on reading them can take over your accounts.
rules.fix: Only allow if the add-on's purpose genuinely requires it, and never combined with network access.

rules.title: Contains a hard-coded secret or API key
rules.explain: A real key is written directly into the file. Anyone who sees the file can use it, and the add-on author may be using your account or theirs in ways you can't see.
rules.fix: Remove the key, rotate it immediately, and load secrets from environment variables or a secret manager.

rules.title: Downloads and runs a script from the internet
rules.explain: Piping a downloaded script straight into a shell runs whatever the server sends - today or after it changes.
rules.fix: Download, read and pin the script instead of piping it into a shell.

rules.title: Opens a remote control connection (reverse shell)
rules.explain: This pattern gives a remote attacker a live command line on your computer.
rules.fix: Do not install. If found on your machine, disconnect and investigate.

rules.title: Destructive delete command
rules.explain: Commands like this can wipe your home folder or whole disk.
rules.fix: Never let an agent run broad delete commands without confirmation.

rules.title: Runs dynamic or shell code
rules.explain: Running shell commands or dynamically built code means the add-on can do anything your user account can do.
rules.fix: Confirm the commands are fixed and safe, not built from untrusted input.

rules.title: Changes permissions or installs persistence
rules.explain: Editing startup files, scheduled tasks or SSH authorized keys lets something keep running or keep access after you stop using it.
rules.fix: An add-on should not modify system startup or access settings.

rules.title: Turns off safety confirmations
rules.explain: Disabling permission prompts or sandboxes means the AI can take any action without asking you first.
rules.fix: Keep confirmations on, especially for tools that write, delete, pay or send.

rules.title: Tries to plant long-term memory
rules.explain: Planting instructions in the AI's memory makes an attack survive into future conversations.
rules.fix: Review and clear the AI's saved memory after using untrusted add-ons.

rules.title: Talks to a raw IP address
rules.explain: Connecting to a bare IP address instead of a named service is unusual for legitimate tools and common in malware.
rules.fix: Find out who owns that server.

rules.title: Uses unencrypted http:// for a remote address
rules.explain: Data sent over plain http can be read or changed by anyone on the network path.
rules.fix: Use https://.

rules.title: Large encoded blob
rules.explain: Long encoded strings can hide code or instructions from human reviewers.
rules.fix: Decode it and check what it contains.

HS-UNI-001.title: Hidden invisible text (Unicode tag characters)
HS-UNI-001.explain: The file contains invisible characters that spell out hidden text. People can't see it, but the AI can read it - a known way to smuggle instructions past reviewers.
HS-UNI-001.fix: Do not install. The decoded hidden text is shown in the finding.

HS-UNI-002.title: Invisible zero-width characters
HS-UNI-002.explain: Zero-width characters are invisible. They are sometimes harmless, but can be used to hide or split words so filters miss them.
HS-UNI-002.fix: Remove them unless you know why they are there.

HS-UNI-003.title: Text-direction override characters (Trojan Source)
HS-UNI-003.explain: Bidirectional override characters make text display differently from how it is actually read by machines, hiding malicious content in plain sight.
HS-UNI-003.fix: Remove them; legitimate code and instructions don't need them.

HS-COMBO-001.title: Reads private data AND can send data out
HS-COMBO-001.explain: The same add-on both touches sensitive data and contains a way to send data out. This combination is exactly what data theft looks like.
HS-COMBO-001.fix: Do not install unless you fully understand and trust both parts.

HS-MCP-001.title: Package version not pinned
HS-MCP-001.explain: This server is downloaded fresh each time without a fixed version. If the package is later hijacked or changes behaviour, you get the new version automatically - a 'rug pull'.
HS-MCP-001.fix: Pin an exact version, e.g. package@1.2.3.

HS-MCP-002.title: Secret written directly in the config
HS-MCP-002.explain: A token or key is stored in plain text in the config file, where other tools, backups or repos can leak it.
HS-MCP-002.fix: Move it to an environment variable or secret manager and rotate the key.

HS-MCP-003.title: Remote server over unencrypted http
HS-MCP-003.explain: Your AI's tool calls and results travel unencrypted to a remote server.

HS-MCP-004.title: Gives access to your whole disk or home folder
HS-MCP-004.explain: The server is pointed at a very broad location, so the AI can read (and maybe change) far more than the task needs.
HS-MCP-004.fix: Point it at only the specific project folder it needs.

HS-MCP-005.title: Container runs with dangerous host access
HS-MCP-005.explain: Privileged containers, host networking or mounting the whole host filesystem remove most of the protection a container gives.
HS-MCP-005.fix: Drop --privileged / --network host and mount only what is needed, read-only where possible.

HS-MCP-006.title: Uses mcp-remote bridge
HS-MCP-006.explain: mcp-remote bridges to a remote server. Older versions had a serious command-injection flaw (CVE-2025-6514) triggerable by a malicious server.
HS-MCP-006.fix: Pin to the latest mcp-remote version and only connect to servers you trust.

HS-MCP-007.title: Connects to a third-party remote server
HS-MCP-007.explain: Your AI's requests and the data in them will be sent to this remote service.
HS-MCP-007.fix: Make sure you trust the operator and understand what data it receives.

HS-MCP-008.title: Tools auto-approved without confirmation
HS-MCP-008.explain: Tools listed here run without asking you first.

HS-N8N-001.title: Workflow runs shell commands
HS-N8N-001.explain: An Execute Command node runs commands directly on the n8n server.
HS-N8N-001.fix: Make sure the command is fixed and never built from incoming data.

HS-N8N-002.title: Code node uses system access
HS-N8N-002.explain: A Code node loads system modules (shell, filesystem) or reads server environment variables, which can expose secrets or run commands.
HS-N8N-002.fix: Review the code; remove system access unless essential.

HS-N8N-003.title: Public webhook with no authentication
HS-N8N-003.explain: Anyone who finds this webhook URL can trigger the workflow.
HS-N8N-003.fix: Add header or basic authentication to the webhook node.

HS-N8N-004.title: AI agent mixes untrusted input, private data and outbound actions
HS-N8N-004.explain: This workflow's AI agent receives outside content (emails, webhooks, web pages), can reach private data, and can send data out. Together these let an attacker steer the agent into leaking data - the 'lethal trifecta'.
HS-N8N-004.fix: Remove one of the three, or require human approval before outbound actions.

HS-SKILL-001.title: Skill can run any shell command
HS-SKILL-001.explain: The skill allows the Bash tool without restricting which commands it may run.
HS-SKILL-001.fix: Restrict it, e.g. Bash(git status:*), to only what the skill needs.
